abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems enhance large language models (LLMs) by integrating external knowledge sources, enabling more accurate and contextually relevant responses tailored to user needs. However, existing RAG systems have significant limitations, including reliance on flat data representations and inadequate contextual awareness, which can lead to fragmented answers that fail to capture complex inter-dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose LightRAG, which incorporates graph structures into text indexing and retrieval processes. This innovative framework employs a dual-level retrieval system that enhances comprehensive information retrieval from both low-level and high-level knowledge discovery. Additionally, the integration of graph structures with vector representations facilitates efficient retrieval of related entities and their relationships, significantly improving response times while maintaining contextual relevance. This capability is further enhanced by an incremental update algorithm that ensures the timely integration of new data, allowing the system to remain effective and responsive in rapidly changing data environments. Extensive experimental validation demonstrates considerable improvements in retrieval accuracy and efficiency compared to existing approaches. We have made our LightRAG open-source and available at the link: https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG.

sections.body: The introduction argues that existing RAG systems rely on flat data representations and lack the contextual awareness to connect entities and their interrelations, which can produce fragmented answers. It proposes LightRAG, which adds graph structures to text indexing and retrieval. The authors name three challenges: comprehensive information retrieval, enhanced retrieval efficiency, and rapid adaptation to new data. LightRAG pairs low-level retrieval for specific entities and relationships with high-level retrieval for broader themes. Its contributions are stated as a graph-empowered RAG system, a dual-level retrieval approach with graph-enhanced indexing, and an incremental update algorithm. The introduction says the experiments cover retrieval accuracy, model ablation, response efficiency, and adaptability, but reports no numbers here.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing RAG systems rely on flat representations and produce fragmented answers, so the paper proposes graph-based indexing with incremental updates.

sections.body: This section defines RAG formally as a framework with a generation module and a retrieval module. The retrieval module has a data indexer, which builds a data structure from the external database, and a data retriever, which compares the query against the indexed data. The generation module then produces a response from the query and the retrieved information. The section sets three targets: comprehensive information retrieval that extracts global information, efficient and low-cost retrieval for a high volume of queries, and fast adaptation to data changes. No experiments are reported in this section.
sections.heading: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
sections.headline: The paper formalizes RAG as indexing and retrieval followed by generation, and sets three design goals for an efficient system.

sections.body: LightRAG segments documents into chunks and uses an LLM to extract entities and relationships, building a knowledge graph. An LLM profiling function generates a key-value pair for each entity and relation, and a deduplication step merges identical items across chunks. For a new document, the incremental update algorithm applies the same indexing and takes the union of the old and new node and edge sets, which avoids rebuilding the whole index. Retrieval has two levels: low-level retrieval targets specific entities and relations, and high-level retrieval targets broader themes. The algorithm extracts local and global query keywords, matches them through a vector database to entities and relations, and adds the one-hop neighbors of retrieved nodes and edges. The stated index cost is that the LLM is called the total tokens divided by chunk size times.
sections.heading: The LightRAG Architecture
sections.headline: LightRAG builds a knowledge graph with LLM extraction, updates it incrementally, and retrieves through dual-level keyword matching.

sections.body: The evaluation uses four UltraDomain datasets, Agriculture, CS, Legal and Mix, with 125 generated questions per dataset. Baselines are NaiveRAG, RQ-RAG, HyDE and GraphRAG, with GPT-4o-mini as the default model, a chunk size of 1200, and the nano vector database. An LLM judge compares answers pairwise on comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment and overall quality, alternating answer positions to reduce order bias. In Table 1, the overall win rate on Legal is 84.8% for LightRAG and 15.2% for NaiveRAG. The authors note that defining ground truth for high-level queries is difficult, so the LLM-based comparison is the main measure. Table 2 reports costs on the legal dataset, where GraphRAG retrieval uses 610,000 tokens and LightRAG uses fewer than 100 tokens for keyword generation and retrieval.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: LightRAG wins LLM-judged comparisons against four baselines on UltraDomain datasets, and uses far fewer retrieval tokens than GraphRAG.

sections.body: The related work section says current RAG methods embed queries in a vector space and retrieve the top-k contexts from fragmented text chunks, which limits global information. It notes that prior graph-based knowledge representation work lacks dynamic updates to the knowledge graph and relies on brute-force searches for each generated community. The section then groups LLM-for-graph work into three categories: GNNs as prefix, LLMs as prefix, and LLM-graph integration. The authors state that LightRAG addresses the update and search limitations through incremental updates and dual-level retrieval. No experiments are reported in this section.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work finds graph-based RAG lacks dynamic updates, and surveys three ways LLMs are combined with graph data.

sections.body: The conclusion describes LightRAG as a graph-based indexing approach that improves efficiency and comprehension in information retrieval. It says the knowledge graph supports rapid and relevant document retrieval, and that the dual-level retrieval approach extracts both specific and abstract information. The authors state that incremental updates keep the system current and responsive to new information. They conclude that LightRAG excels in efficiency and effectiveness and reduces costs for LLM inference. The conclusion restates these claims without new numbers, and it does not list limitations.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: LightRAG is concluded to improve retrieval speed and quality and cut LLM inference costs through graph indexing and incremental updates.

sections.body: The appendix gives Table 4 dataset statistics: Agriculture has 12 documents and 2,017,886 tokens, CS has 10 documents and 2,306,535 tokens, Legal has 94 documents and 5,081,069 tokens, and Mix has 61 documents and 619,009 tokens. Table 5 compares LightRAG and NaiveRAG on a question about Indigenous perspectives and corporate mergers, where the authors judge the LightRAG answer more comprehensive, diverse and empowering. The appendix also describes the case example of retrieval and generation and gives the prompts used for graph generation, query generation, keyword extraction and RAG evaluation.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, a case study against NaiveRAG, and the prompts for graph generation, query generation, keyword extraction and evaluation.
